To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2.     "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. Since the set is totally ordered, any prefix of \\( a \\) must be comparable. Being the longest in its class, all shorter prefixes would also be in the set due to the total ordering and the properties of equivalence classes.\n\n- **Maintaining Equivalence:** Because each element is the longest in its class, all such classes are respected, ensuring that all prefixes are included as required for the set to be prefix-closed.\n\nThis completes the bi-directional proof, confirming that a set's prefix-closed property is equivalent to being totally ordered by the prefix relation and having each element as the longest in its equivalence class.",

    "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. Since the set is totally ordered, any prefix of \\( a \\) must be comparable. Being the longest in its class, all shorter prefixes would also be in the set due to the total ordering and the properties of equivalence classes.\n\n- **Maintaining Equivalence:** Because each element is the longest in its class, all such classes are respected, ensuring that all prefixes are included as required for the set to be prefix-closed.\n\nThis completes the bi-directional proof, confirming that a set's prefix-closed property is equivalent to being totally ordered by the prefix relation and having each element as the longest in its equivalence class.",

    "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. Since the set is totally ordered, any prefix of \\( a \\) must be comparable. Being the longest in its class, all shorter prefixes would also be in the set due to the total ordering and the properties of equivalence classes.\n\n- **Maintaining Equivalence:** Because each element is the longest in its class, all such classes are respected, ensuring that all prefixes are included as required for the set to be prefix-closed.\n\nThis completes the bi-directional proof, confirming that a set's prefix-closed property is equivalent to being totally ordered by the prefix relation and having each element as the longest in its equivalence class.",

     "/-- Override the Lean 4 pi notation delaborator with one that uses `Π` and prints\ncute binders such as `∀ ε > 0`.\nNote that this takes advantage of the fact that `(x : α) → p x` notation is\nnever used for propositions, so we can match on this result and rewrite it. -/\n@[scoped delab forallE]\ndef delabPi' : Delab := whenPPOption Lean.getPPNotation do\n  -- Use delabForall as a backup if `pp.mathlib.binderPredicates` is false.\n  let stx ← delabPi <|> delabForall\n  -- Replacements\n  let stx : Term ←\n    match stx with\n    | `($group:bracketedBinder → $body) => `(Π $group:bracketedBinder, $body)\n    | _ => pure stx\n  -- Merging\n  match stx with\n  | `(Π $group, Π $groups*, $body) => `(Π $group $groups*, $body)\n  | _ => pure stx"}}],

    "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. Since the set is totally ordered, any prefix of \\( a \\) must be comparable. Being the longest in its class, all shorter prefixes would also be in the set due to the total ordering and the properties of equivalence classes.\n\n- **Maintaining Equivalence:** Because each element is the longest in its class, all such classes are respected, ensuring that all prefixes are included as required for the set to be prefix-closed.\n\nThis completes the bi-directional proof, confirming that a set's prefix-closed property is equivalent to being totally ordered by the prefix relation and having each element as the longest in its equivalence class.",

    "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. Since the set is totally ordered, any prefix of \\( a \\) must be comparable. Being the longest in its class, all shorter prefixes would also be in the set due to the total ordering and the properties of equivalence classes.\n\n- **Maintaining Equivalence:** Because each element is the longest in its class, all such classes are respected, ensuring that all prefixes are included as required for the set to be prefix-closed.\n\nThis completes the bi-directional proof, confirming that a set's prefix-closed property is equivalent to being totally ordered by the prefix relation and having each element as the longest in its equivalence class.",

We aim to show that:\n\\[ (S \\setminus T) \\cup (T \\setminus S) = (S \\cup T) \\setminus (S \\cap T) \\]\n\nTo prove equality between two sets, we demonstrate that each set is a subset of the other.\n\n**First, we show that \\( (S \\setminus T) \\cup (T \\setminus S) \\subseteq (S \\cup T) \\setminus (S \\cap T) \\).**\n\nLet \\( x \\in (S \\setminus T) \\cup (T \\setminus S) \\). Thus, \\( x \\in (S \\cup T) \\setminus (S \\cap T) \\).\n- If \\( x \\in T \\setminus S \\), then \\( x \\in T \\) and \\( x \\notin S \\). Therefore, \\( x \\in S \\cup T \\) (since \\( x \\in T \\)) and \\( x \\notin S \\cap T \\) (since \\( x \\notin S \\)). Therefore, \\( x \\in T \\setminus S \\).\n- Hence, \\( x \\in (S \\setminus T) \\cup (T \\setminus S) \\).\n\nSince every element of \\( (S \\setminus T) \\cup (T \\setminus S) \\) is in \\( (S \\cup T) \\setminus (S \\cap T) \\) and vice versa, the two sets are equal.\n\n**Therefore, we conclude that:**\n\\[ S \\setminus T \\cup T \\setminus S = (S \\cup T) \\setminus (S \\cap T) \\]",

    "This code provides a method to override the Pi notation in Lean's pretty printer, allowing for a more readable and intuitive syntax such as `∀ ε > 0`. By defining a custom delabitation for Pi, it transforms complex Pi expressions into a cleaner universal quantifier (∀) with added clarity and formatting.\n\nTo achieve the desired override of the Pi notation in Lean's pretty printer, the following steps are taken:\n\n1. **Definition of Pi Delabitation**: The `delabPi'` definition is crafted to match any Pi binding in the expression.     "A set is prefix-closed if and only if it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class under the prefix relation.\n\nFirst, we understand that a set is *prefix-closed* if whenever a string is in the set, all its prefixes are also in the set. To characterize this property, we use the prefix relation and equivalence relations.\n\nWe need to prove that a set is prefix-closed if and only if it satisfies two conditions:\n\n1. **Total Order by Prefix Relation**: Any two elements in the set are comparable under the prefix relation. That is, for any two elements \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) in the set, either \\( a \\) is a prefix of \\( b \\) or \\( b \\) is a prefix of \\( a \\).\n\n2. **Equivalence Classes**: Each element in the set belongs to an equivalence class where it is the longest element. This ensures that there are no shorter elements preceding it within its equivalence class.\n\n*Proof Structure:*\n\nWe will prove this equivalence in two directions:\n\n**1. If a set is prefix-closed, then it is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest element of its equivalence class.**\n\n- **Total Order:** Suppose \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are two elements in the prefix-closed set. Without loss of generality, assume \\( a \\) is not a prefix of \\( b \\). Since the set is prefix-closed, \\( a \\) itself is in the set, and therefore should contain \\( a \\) as a prefix if \\( b \\) is also to be in the set. This leads to \\( a \\) being a prefix of either \\( b \\) or vice versa, establishing total order.\n\n- **Longest Element in Equivalence Class:** Consider elements in the set that are prefixes of each other. The longest one cannot be extended further without losing the prefix property. Thus, each equivalence class has a unique longest element, ensuring that each element is the longest in its class.\n\n**2. If a set is totally ordered by the prefix relation and every element is the longest in its equivalence class, then the set is prefix-closed.**\n\n- **Preservation Under Prefixes:** Take any element \\( a \\) in the set. Since the set is totally ordered, any prefix of \\( a \\) must be comparable. Being the longest in its class, all shorter prefixes would also be in the set due to the total ordering and the properties of equivalence classes.\n\n- **Maintaining Equivalence:** Because each element is the longest in its class, all such classes are respected, ensuring that all prefixes are included as required for the set to be prefix-closed.\n\nThis completes the bi-directional proof, confirming that a set's prefix-closed property is equivalent to being totally ordered by the prefix relation and having each element as the longest in its equivalence class.",
